Greg Molnár: “The European gas storage campaign will be more challenging than expected”

By Emese Fabian
May 7, 2026
Facebook
X
WhatsApp
Linkedin
Email
Print

    “The Middle East conflict is profoundly disrupting global gas and LNG markets, affecting supply, prices, and the medium-term outlook,” said Gergely Molnár, Gas Analyst, International Energy Agency (IEA), in his keynote speech at the 7th Budapest LNG Summit.

    He said that last year the key question in the rooms was whether there would be enough demand to absorb all the LNG coming to the market. In fact, in 2025-26, global LNG supply grew by a very strong 10 per cent or 29 BCM. Almost half of this incremental supply came from one single plant, in Louisiana. The increase provided downward pressure on natural gas prices, with both TTF Europe and JKM Asia trading about 25 per cent below their levels from the previous year for the October – February period.

    It was expect that this trend would continue in 2026. “Our expectation was that global LNG supply will increase by 7 per cent or 42 billion cubic meters. And the good news is that out of these 42 billion cubic meters, about 40 billion cubic meters is still expected to come to the market.”

    However, geopolitical forces are once again distorting the functioning of the global gas market. Back in 2025, around 90 per cent of the exit flows from the Strait went to Asia, accounting for more than 25 per cent of the region’s LNG supply. In contrast, only about 10 per cent of the exit flows went to Europe, accounting for roughly 3 per cent of the region’s natural gas demand.

    “There is a tendency in Europe to say that this is mainly an Asian problem, but the thing is that we are living in an increasingly globalised gas market. In fact, when we look at the correlation between Asian and European gas prices, we see that this increased from around 15 per cent back in 2015 to over 95 per cent in 2025, highlighting the increasingly interlinked nature of the two regional gas markets.”

    In the first two days after the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, TTF in Europe increased by around 70 per cent, while JKM prices more than doubled over the same period of time, and both of them reached their highest levels since the 2022-23 gas price shock. 

    The loadings from Qatar and the Emirates were down by approximately 18 billion cubic meters, and this has been partly offset by the increases in other markets, supported by new LNG capacity, but also very importantly by improving LNG supply availability at certain major producers. 

    One key question ahead of the summer will be Europe’s storage injection campaign. Reaching 90 per cent fill levels would require 10 billion cubic meters of additional storage injections compared to the summer of 2023, while reaching 80 per cent fill levels would require similar injection rates as last year. “Now, when we are looking back to April, we see that injections stood about 20 per cent below their last year levels. So we are not really on track at the moment to reach the 90 per cent fill levels. And this is reflective of the tighter supply conditions, but also the negative seasonal spread which are reducing the commercial incentive to put natural gas into underground storage. So it seems that the European storage campaign will be more challenging and probably more expensive than expected.”

    Looking at the global LNG supply over the 2026 to 2030 period, he said that approximately 120 billion cubic meters of LNG has already been lost due to the Middle East conflict. “This accounts for roughly 15 per cent of the new cumulative LNG supply expected to come to the market. In other words, the strong increases in new LNG capacity, especially in the United States, will offset these losses. However, the effect of the unfolding LNG wave will be delayed by at least two years, meaning that the market will be tighter for longer than previously expected.”
